reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, restricting skull growth perpendicular to the fused suture and producing a characteristic head shape
Sagittal suture fusion gives a long, narrow head (scaphocephaly) and is the most common single-suture form
The head-shape abnormality is typically present at or soon after birth and progresses, unlike positional plagiocephaly which usually improves with repositioning
A palpable ridge along the affected suture and an abnormal skull contour are important clinical clues
Most single-suture cases are non-syndromic and isolated, but multi-suture or syndromic forms (such as Apert, Crouzon, or Pfeiffer) carry higher risks and associated anomalies
Multi-suture involvement can raise intracranial pressure and threaten vision and neurodevelopment, so fundoscopy and developmental monitoring are important
Cranial CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirms the diagnosis and defines the sutures involved when clinical assessment is uncertain
Treatment is usually surgical remodelling to correct the deformity and allow normal brain growth, with timing and approach tailored to the sutures affected and the child's age
reference.pathophysiology: Craniosynostosis arises when one or more cranial sutures fuse prematurely, before the underlying brain has finished its rapid early growth. Because bone cannot expand across the fused suture, compensatory growth occurs at the remaining open sutures, distorting the skull into a predictable shape determined by which suture is involved. When several sutures fuse, the overall cranial volume may become inadequate for the growing brain, leading to raised intracranial pressure. Syndromic forms are often driven by identifiable genetic mutations affecting fibroblast growth factor signalling and are associated with midface and limb anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Microcephaly with a small but normally shaped skull
Metabolic bone disease affecting the skull
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of head shape, suture ridging, and head circumference trend
Cranial CT with 3D reconstruction to confirm fused sutures and plan surgery
Fundoscopy to detect papilloedema suggesting raised intracranial pressure
Genetic assessment when a syndromic form or multiple sutures are involved
redFlags: Multi-suture fusion with signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema
Progressive skull deformity with developmental delay or visual compromise
Features of a craniofacial syndrome with airway or midface concerns
Rapidly abnormal head growth or a bulging appearance suggesting elevated pressure
reference.prognosis: Isolated single-suture craniosynostosis generally has an excellent outcome after timely surgical correction; multi-suture and syndromic forms are more complex, carry a greater risk of raised intracranial pressure and neurodevelopmental problems, and often require staged, multidisciplinary management.
pitfalls: Confusing positional plagiocephaly, which improves with repositioning, with true synostosis
Missing raised intracranial pressure in multi-suture disease by omitting fundoscopy
Underestimating associated anomalies and genetic implications in syndromic cases
Delaying referral so that the optimal surgical window is missed
management: Surgical correction by cranial vault remodelling, or minimally invasive strip craniectomy with post-operative helmet moulding, to relieve constraint and correct skull shape
Tailor the timing and technique to the suture involved, the child's age and the presence of raised intracranial pressure
Monitor for and treat raised intracranial pressure, using staged surgery in multi-suture and syndromic forms
Fundoscopy and ophthalmological surveillance for papilloedema and visual compromise
Developmental surveillance with early intervention for neurodevelopmental delay
Genetic assessment and counselling for syndromic and multi-suture forms such as fibroblast growth factor receptor-related Apert, Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes
Multidisciplinary craniofacial team management including airway and midface assessment in syndromic cases
